title: Argent Payments - Private VPC discovery
summary: Intro discovery for Argent Payments exploring Redwood Private (VPC) deployment. Customer walked through current infra, VPC topology, CIDR ranges, and compliance constraints. Main asks: peering options, private endpoints (PrivateLink), regional availability, egress controls, and KMS integration. Next steps: send peering diagram and network checklist, pricing estimate for private deployment, and schedule technical deep-dive with infra team.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-11 14:00 PDT
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (CTO, Argent), Owen Brooks (Infra Lead), Sara Klein (Security)

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm lena from redwood, quick roll call?
[00:06] Priya Patel: hi priya here, i'm the cto at argent, thanks for doing this.
[00:09] Owen Brooks: owen infra lead, good to meet you.
[00:11] Sara Klein: sara in security and compliance.
[00:13] Lena Ortiz: awesome, i'll hand to marcus for a quick run through what we'll cover  network options for private deployment, peering, private endpoints, k-m-s integration, and region constraints.
[00:22] Marcus Chen: yep hi all, short agenda, first gather your current topology, then explain redwood private options: vpc peering, aws privatelink/stuff, and private endpoints, tradeoffs on egress and nat, and then q&a.
[00:32] Priya Patel: perfect. quick context: Argent is a payments platform, we have PCI scope on some services, we run primarily in us-east-1 and us-west-2 but latency to eu-west-1 matters for some customers. Our compliance folks want all model inference to run in our VPC or a dedicated private deployment. we want to avoid open internet egress for token data.
[00:50] Marcus Chen: understood. two common patterns: 1) vpc peering to redwood-managed vpc where we host the inference cluster, 2) private endpoints / privatelink where customers keep control and the service is exposed over private endpoints. each has tradeoffs re routing, transitive peering, and bandwidth.
[01:07] Owen Brooks: quick clar  are you expecting us to hand over CIDR blocks for peering, or can we use private endpoints so we don't have to change our route tables too much?
[01:15] Marcus Chen: good q. with vpc peering we need your CIDRs and we set up peering connections; you update route-tables to send traffic to redwood. with privatelink (aws privatelink / gcp psc equivalent) you create an interface endpoint in your subnet and traffic stays on aws backbone  less route table surgery and no transitive peering issues.
[01:33] Sara Klein: from a security perspective we prefer privatelink because it minimizes exposure and we can lock down SGs. also need support for customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest, and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[01:46] Lena Ortiz: good to note. redwood private supports kms integration  we can bring-your-own-kms or use a customer-managed key in your account depending on the deployment profile. marcus, can you expand?
[01:55] Marcus Chen: sure, two patterns we use: 1) host all resources in our managed account but with a cross-account KMS key where you control key policy  this requires some IAM setup; 2) fully customer-managed deployment where the inference nodes run in your account (we provide an appliance/ami or helm chart) and you keep keys and kms. first is faster to stand up, second gives max control.
[02:20] Owen Brooks: better to understand both. for the first option, will logs ever transit to redwood-managed endpoints? our compliance team needs log retention in our splunk.
[02:28] Marcus Chen: logs can be configured either way  we can forward audit logs to your s3/logging endpoints, and we can also provide read-only access for support. for the hosted-in-customer-peering model we typically push logs to your s3 via cross-account write.
[02:44] Priya Patel: region question  if our primary compute is in us-east-1 and some customers need eu-west-1 residency, can redwood provision private deployments in both regions?
[02:53] Marcus Chen: yes. Redwood Private can be deployed per-region. caveat: model artifacts and snapshot replication between regions takes time and we can pre-stage models in the regions you need. ROI wise there is cost overhead for multi-region dedicated clusters.
[03:08] Sara Klein: do you have SOC2 / ISO docs we can share with procurement?
[03:11] Lena Ortiz: absolutely, i'll attach our SOC2 report and security whitepaper, and our network checklist.
[03:16] Sara Klein: and what about HSM vs KMS? some of our tokenization keys must live in an HSM.
[03:22] Marcus Chen: we support HSM-backed keys via customer-managed HSMs, generally through cloud provider HSM offerings (AWS CloudHSM) when you do a fully customer-managed deployment. if you want us to manage it in our account we can integrate with third-party HSMs but that adds procurement steps.
[03:38] Owen Brooks: can you talk a little about egress? we have strict firewall requirements and everything must egress through our nat gateway with egress filtering.
[03:45] Marcus Chen: for privatelink traffic stays in the provider network; with peering traffic flows over the peering connection and egress is controllable from your side. if you require all egress to go via your nat, we can route that; for some topologies we recommend hairpinning through a transit VPC or using a proxy appliance. we'll include diagram examples.
[04:05] Priya Patel: what about simultaneous connections  are there limit concerns? we expect spikes during batch reconciliation runs, sometimes hundreds of concurrent request streams.
[04:14] Marcus Chen: dedicated capacity supports predictable throughput with reserved GPU pools; we can size for burst and autoscale rules. with privatelink the throughput is bounded by endpoint ENI quotas and your subnets; we can plan for large ENIs and scale across availability zones. we'll work with you on limits.
[04:32] Lena Ortiz: quick interjection  we also have Redwood Optimize suggestions for batching/caching to lower per-token costs if you have burst windows.
[04:38] Priya Patel: good. another operational item: certificate rotation and mTLS  can we enforce mutual TLS for inbound call auth?
[04:46] Marcus Chen: yes we support mTLS for service-to-service calls in private deployments. if you want to use client certs we can add that in the ingress layer and rotate via your cert manager.
[04:56] Owen Brooks: any special firewall ports or ephemeral ports we should expect?
[04:59] Marcus Chen: primarily HTTPS over 443. grpc streams may use persistent TCP, but still port 443. for internal control plane you may need ports for ssh for support if you allow it, but that's optional. we'll list exact ports in the checklist.
[05:14] Sara Klein: how about RBAC/SSO integration for the console and audit trails?
[05:18] Lena Ortiz: we support SAML/SSO and SCIM for provisioning, and audit logs are available both in-console and exportable to your logging endpoints.
[05:26] Priya Patel: any sticky notes on cross-account peering and transitive routes? we have a transit gateway already  would that simplify things?
[05:34] Marcus Chen: transit gateway often simplifies large org topologies. we can peer to an account attached to the transit gateway, or set up privatelink endpoints in each VPC you want. note that transit gateway has bandwidth and route limits to consider. we'll include TGW patterns in the diagram.
[05:50] Owen Brooks: what's the typical timeline to get a pilot up and running if we want a model in us-east-1 with privatelink and KMS in our account?
[05:57] Marcus Chen: for privatelink + cross-account kms + privatelink endpoint, typical pilot is 2-3 weeks: initial network exchange and testing in 3-5 days, staging cluster in a week, and verification/test in the second week. if you want fully customer-managed on-premish, add extra time for install and validation.
[06:13] Priya Patel: budgetary question  private deployments are expensive. can you give a ballpark for a small pilot?
[06:19] Lena Ortiz: I'll send a ballpark monthly committed pricing. for a small pilot you're looking at reserved capacity for a few GPUs plus networking  i'll include cost ranges in the doc.
[06:28] Sara Klein: any data residency guarantees we can sign for? some EU customers require data to never leave EU.
[06:33] Marcus Chen: yes we can commit to region pinning and not replicate artifacts outside pinned regions. that's part of dedicated/private SLAs. we'll need to agree on model artifact management and backup policies.
[06:46] Priya Patel: ok makes sense. one more network detail  we run strict ephemeral port blocking on our subnets; will that impact the privatelink ENI health checks?
[06:55] Marcus Chen: health checks are https calls, so as long as 443 is open to the endpoint ENI it's fine. some control signals use ephemeral ranges but we can do keepalives over 443. we'll confirm in the checklist.
[07:06] Owen Brooks: can redwood provide a CloudFormation/Terraform snippet to create the endpoint and required SGs?
[07:10] Marcus Chen: yes, i'll share sample terraform and cfn templates  that'll be one of the artifacts we commit to send.
[07:16] Lena Ortiz: recap to make sure we captured asks: 1) network diagram and checklist, 2) sample terraform/cfn, 3) pricing estimate, 4) SOC2 and KMS/HSM guide, 5) schedule deep-dive. everyone good?
[07:27] Priya Patel: yep that's it.
[07:29] Owen Brooks: yep.
[07:30] Sara Klein: good.
[07:31] Lena Ortiz: great  i'll follow up after the call with links. Marcus anything else?
[07:35] Marcus Chen: just one note, sometimes transcription and product names get munged  if you see 'redwood private' spelled weird in these notes, that's normal, we'll attach clean docs.
[07:44] Priya Patel: (laughs) understood. thanks both.
[07:47] Lena Ortiz: thanks everyone. we'll target the artifacts by the dates we discussed. thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
